issues.legal_issue: A licensing law does not confer arbitrary discretion when, read as a whole, it guides the licensing authority by the applicant’s control of the premises, good behaviour, and ability to prevent drunkenness and disorder.
material_facts: The applicant challenged the law governing licences for eating houses as conferring unguided power to grant or refuse a licence.
The law provided for licensing to secure the good behaviour of keepers and to prevent drunkenness and disorder among those using the premises.
The Court read the licensing provision as requiring the applicant to have actual and effective control and possession of the premises.
issues.conclusion: The licensing provision, fairly read as a whole, guided the Commissioner by those criteria and did not confer arbitrary or uncanalised discretion or impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on business.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 19(1)(g) and 19(6) of the Constitution, a restriction on the right to carry on business must be reasonable. A pre-Constitution statute must be read as a whole and fairly; it need not be struck down merely because its language does not expressly recite constitutional considerations. Section 39 of the Calcutta Police Act, 1866, read as a whole, guides licensing by the keeper’s actual and effective control of the premises, good behaviour, and ability to prevent drunkenness and disorder. The Court relied on the approach to reasonableness in State of Madras v. V. G. Row and Nagendra Nath Bora v. The Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals, Assam, and distinguished Rustom Jamshed Irani v. Harley Kennedy as inapplicable.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_business_lic: A person challenged a licensing scheme as restricting the right to carry on a business.
predicates.licensing_linked_to_public_order: The licensing scheme linked its conditions to securing keepers’ good behaviour and preventing disorder among people using the premises.
predicates.applicant_required_to_control_premises: The licensing scheme, read as a whole, required the applicant to have actual and effective control of the premises.

issues.definition: When a business-licensing challenge concerns a scheme tied to public-order aims and requiring the applicant to control the premises, the licensing discretion is not arbitrary or unreasonable.

issues.legal_issue: The omission of a pre-decision hearing and a duty to communicate reasons does not, in every licensing scheme, make the restriction on business unreasonable.
material_facts: The licensing provision did not require the Commissioner to hear an applicant before deciding an application or to communicate reasons for refusal.
The Commissioner’s decision was an administrative decision based on his satisfaction about the applicant and the prevention of drunkenness and disorder.
The applicant could seek review under Article 226 if the refusal rested on extraneous or irrelevant grounds.
issues.conclusion: In the setting of this licensing provision, the absence of a hearing and a requirement to communicate reasons did not make the restriction unconstitutional.
issues.legal_principle: The reasonableness of a restriction must be assessed in the setting of the particular law, including its procedural features; no general rule makes every licensing provision invalid for omitting a hearing or communicated reasons. The Court treated the decision under section 39 of the Calcutta Police Act, 1866, as administrative rather than judicial, while requiring the Commissioner to act reasonably. It relied on State of Madras v. V. G. Row, Nagendra Nath Bora v. The Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals, Assam, Nakkuda Ali v. M. F. De S. Jayaratne, and Express Newspapers (P.) Ltd. v. The Union of India, and noted the availability of review under Article 226 of the Constitution.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_business_licensing and no_predecision_hearing and no_communicated_reasons and administrative_licensing_decision and judicial_review_available

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_business_lic: A person challenged a licensing scheme as restricting the right to carry on a business.
predicates.no_predecision_hearing: The licensing scheme did not require the authority to hear an applicant before deciding the application.
predicates.no_communicated_reasons: The licensing scheme did not require the authority to communicate its reasons for refusing an application.
predicates.administrative_licensing_decision: The licensing authority made an administrative decision rather than deciding a dispute through a judicial process.
predicates.judicial_review_available: The affected applicant could seek judicial review of a refusal alleged to rest on irrelevant grounds.

issues.definition: Where a business-licensing challenge concerns an administrative decision and judicial review is available, the absence of a pre-decision hearing and communicated reasons does not itself make the restriction unreasonable.

issues.legal_issue: A refusal of a licence is not mala fide merely because the applicant disputes the stated reasons and alleges that the authority was annoyed by the applicant’s resort to court.
material_facts: The Commissioner refused the applicant’s licence on the stated grounds concerning the applicant’s antecedents and conduct and the ability to prevent drunkenness and disorder.
The applicant alleged that the reasons were incorrect and that the Commissioner was annoyed because the applicant had approached the High Court.
The applicant did not allege personal animus by the Commissioner or that the Commissioner was favouring the previous keeper.
issues.conclusion: The allegations did not establish that the refusal was mala fide.
issues.legal_principle: A claim of mala fides requires more than disagreement with the stated reasons or an assertion that the authority was annoyed by prior litigation; the Court found those allegations insufficient in the absence of an allegation of personal animus or favouritism.

rule.if: licence_refusal_challenged_as_mala_fide and reasons_disputed and alleged_annoyance_from_litigation and no_personal_animus_or_favouritism_alleged

predicates.licence_refusal_challenged_as_mala_fide: An applicant challenged the refusal of a business licence as having been made in bad faith.
predicates.reasons_disputed: The applicant claimed that the authority’s stated reasons for refusing the licence were incorrect.
predicates.alleged_annoyance_from_litigation: The applicant claimed that the authority was annoyed because the applicant had previously sought relief in court.
predicates.no_personal_animus_or_favouritism_allege: The applicant did not allege that the authority had personal animus against the applicant or was favouring another person.

issues.definition: When a licence refusal is challenged as bad faith on the basis of disputed reasons and alleged annoyance from litigation, without an allegation of personal animus or favouritism, bad faith is not established.
